title: Reversible Changes and Dissolving
kicker: Cambridge Primary Checkpoint · Science 0097 · Stage 6 · Chemistry
summary: Learn which physical changes can be reversed and how, what really happens when a solid dissolves, and why solids dissolve faster and more in hot water — explained with the particle model.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: Spot physical changes that can be reversed (undone) and describe how to reverse them, for example melting and freezing, evaporating and condensing, dissolving and evaporating the water away. (6Cc.01)
Describe how the temperature of a liquid changes how solids dissolve in it, and explain this using the particle model. (6Cc.02)

blocks.text: 2. Physical changes and reversible changes

In a **physical change** no new substance is made. Ice is still water; melted chocolate is still chocolate; salt in water is still salt and water. Because the substance is still there, many physical changes are **reversible** — we can get the original substance back.

In a **chemical change** (a chemical reaction) new substances are made, for example when wood burns to ash and smoke. Most chemical changes are **irreversible**. You will study these on the Chemical Reactions page.

blocks.text: **Careful:** not every physical change is easy to reverse. Tearing paper or crushing a can are physical changes (no new substance), but you cannot easily put them back as they were. In Checkpoint questions, "reversible" means you can get the **same substance** back again.

blocks.title: The one test to use
blocks.text: Ask two questions: (1) Is a new substance made? If yes → chemical change, usually irreversible. (2) If no new substance is made, can I get the original back by heating, cooling, filtering, evaporating or using a magnet? If yes → reversible physical change.
3. Dissolving

When you stir sugar into water, the sugar seems to disappear. It has not gone — it has **dissolved**. The sugar is the **solute**, the water is the **solvent** and the sweet clear liquid is a **solution**. You can still taste the sugar, and if you let the water evaporate, the sugar is left behind. This proves dissolving is a **reversible** change.

items: **Soluble** substances dissolve in water: salt, sugar, instant coffee, washing powder.
**Insoluble** substances do not dissolve in water: sand, chalk, flour (it makes a cloudy mixture), pepper.
A solution is **clear** (you can see through it), even if it is coloured, like weak tea or blue copper sulfate solution. A cloudy mixture means some solid has not dissolved.

blocks.title: Dissolving is NOT melting
blocks.text: Melting needs only one substance and heat: solid ice → liquid water. Dissolving needs two substances: a solute and a solvent. Sugar in tea dissolves; it does not melt. Writing "the sugar melted" loses the mark.
4. Mass does not change when a solid dissolves

The solute particles are still there, only spread out, so the **mass of the solution = mass of solvent + mass of solute**. If you dissolve 20 g of salt in 100 g of water, the solution has a mass of 120 g. Nothing is lost.
5. Getting the substances back (reversing)

items: **Filtering** separates an **insoluble** solid from a liquid. Pour the mixture through filter paper in a funnel. The solid (the residue) stays in the paper; the liquid (the filtrate) passes through.

**Evaporating** separates a **dissolved** solid from its solution. Heat the solution gently in an evaporating basin, or leave it in a warm place. The water becomes water vapour and the solid is left as crystals.
To collect the **water** as well, the water vapour must be cooled so it **condenses** back into a liquid (this is how solar stills make clean water from salty water).
Filtering cannot separate salt from water — the salt particles are so small that they pass through the filter paper with the water.

blocks.text: 6. The particle model of dissolving
Scientists use a **model** to explain dissolving: everything is made of tiny particles that are always moving. In a liquid the particles touch but slide past each other.

blocks.caption: Model of dissolving: water particles knock sugar particles off the crystal; the sugar particles spread out in the spaces between the water particles.

items: Water particles are always moving and bump into the surface of the sugar crystal.
The bumps pull sugar particles away from the crystal one by one.
The sugar particles spread out and mix between the water particles, so the crystal gets smaller and smaller until it cannot be seen.
The sugar particles are still there (the mass is the same), just too spread out to see.

blocks.text: 7. How temperature affects dissolving
For most solids, a **higher temperature** of the liquid has two effects:

items: **The solid dissolves faster** (it takes less time to dissolve).
**More solid can dissolve** in the same volume of liquid before the solution is saturated.

blocks.caption: Longer arrows = faster particles. In hot water the particles move faster, so they hit the crystal more often and harder.

blocks.text: **Particle explanation:** when the water is heated, its particles get more energy and **move faster**. Fast particles hit the solid **more often and with more force**, so sugar particles are pulled away from the crystal and spread out **more quickly**. Because the particles are moving faster, there is also room for more sugar particles to spread out among them, so more sugar dissolves before the solution becomes saturated.

Other things also make a solid dissolve faster — **stirring** and using **smaller pieces** (powder instead of a cube). In a fair test about temperature, these must be kept the **same** (control variables).

blocks.text: **Reading the graph:** as the temperature goes up, the time to dissolve goes down. The curve gets less steep at higher temperatures: going from 20 °C to 30 °C saves 45 s, but going from 50 °C to 60 °C saves only 15 s.

blocks.title: الفكرة باختصار
blocks.text: الذوبان تغير فيزيائي عكسي: السكر لا يختفي، بل تتوزع جسيماته بين جسيمات الماء، ونستطيع استرجاعه بتبخير الماء. كلما زادت درجة حرارة الماء تتحرك جسيماته أسرع، فتصطدم بالسكر أكثر وبقوة أكبر، فيذوب أسرع ويذوب منه كمية أكبر. انتبه: السكر "يذوب" (dissolves) ولا "ينصهر" (melts).
8. Worked examples

**Worked example 1** — Here are five changes: melting wax, burning wax, dissolving coffee in hot water, freezing orange juice, cooking an egg. Write down the **three** changes that are reversible. [2 marks]

items: Ask for each one: is a new substance made? Burning wax makes new gases (carbon dioxide and water vapour) and cooking an egg changes it into a new substance — both are chemical and irreversible.
The others make no new substance: melting wax (cool it → solid wax again), dissolving coffee (evaporate the water → coffee left), freezing juice (warm it → liquid juice).
**Answer:** melting wax, dissolving coffee, freezing orange juice. (2 marks for all three correct, 1 mark for two correct.)

blocks.text: **Worked example 2** — Omar puts 200 g of water in a beaker. He dissolves 25 g of salt in it. (a) What is the mass of the salt solution? [1] (b) Explain your answer. [1]

items: (a) mass of solution = mass of water + mass of salt = 200 + 25 = **225 g**.
(b) The salt particles are still there, spread out between the water particles; nothing is lost, so the mass does not change.
**Common mistake:** writing 200 g because "the salt disappeared". Dissolved substances still have mass.

blocks.text: **Worked example 3** — Laila has a mixture of sand and salt. Describe how she can get **dry sand** and **salt crystals** from the mixture. [3 marks]

items: Add water and stir — the salt dissolves, the sand does not. (1 mark)
Filter the mixture — the sand stays in the filter paper (dry it in a warm place). (1 mark)
Evaporate the water from the salt solution that passed through — salt crystals are left. (1 mark)
**Exam tip:** always say what each step separates and where each substance ends up.

blocks.text: **Worked example 4** — Use the graph in section 7. (a) How long did the sugar take to dissolve at 40 °C? [1] (b) Describe the pattern. [1] (c) Explain the pattern using the particle model. [2]

items: (a) Go up from 40 on the temperature axis to the line, then across: **80 s**.
(b) The higher the temperature, the shorter the time to dissolve (the sugar dissolves faster).
(c) At a higher temperature the water particles move faster (1); they hit the sugar more often/harder so sugar particles are pulled away and spread out more quickly (1).
**Common mistake:** "the sugar particles melt". Particles never melt, and the sugar is dissolving, not melting.

blocks.text: **Worked example 5** — Youssef predicts: "More sugar will dissolve in 100 ml of water at 70 °C than at 30 °C." Is his prediction correct? Give a reason. [2 marks]

items: Yes, his prediction is correct (1).

Reason: for most solids, more solute can dissolve in hotter water before the solution is saturated, because the faster-moving particles make room for more sugar particles to spread out among them (1).
**To test it:** add sugar one level spoonful at a time, stirring, until no more dissolves; count the spoonfuls at each temperature, using the same volume of water each time.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Saying a solid "melts" in water — the correct word is **dissolves**.
Saying the solute "disappears" or "is lost" — it is still there; the mass of the solution includes it.
Thinking filtering can remove salt from salt water — filtering only removes **insoluble** solids. Use **evaporation** for dissolved solids.
Mixing up solute (the solid) and solvent (the liquid). Memory trick: the solv**ent** is the liquid that the solute **ent**ers.
Explaining with "the heat melts the sugar" instead of "the particles move faster and hit the solid more often".
Calling every physical change reversible — torn paper cannot be put back; ask whether you can get the same substance back.

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: **Sort or tick**: which changes are reversible? Look for new substances (burning, cooking, rusting = not reversible).
**Calculate a mass**: water + solid = solution. Show the addition, write the unit g.
**Describe how to separate**: give the method (filter / evaporate / magnet) AND what happens to each substance.

**Investigation questions**: name the variable you change (temperature), the one you measure (time to dissolve or amount dissolved) and two you keep the same (volume of water, mass and type of sugar, size of pieces, amount of stirring).
**Explain with particles**: for 2 marks you need two ideas — particles move faster, and so they hit/pull solute particles away more often so it dissolves faster.
Read graph values carefully: check what one small square is worth before you answer.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Reversible changes and dissolving — practice
blocks.intro: Answer every part. Type short answers in the box; for longer answers write yours on paper, then mark it with the mark scheme.

questions.q: Which of these is a reversible change?
questions.e: Melting butter makes no new substance; cooling it makes solid butter again. Burning, frying and rusting all make new substances, so they cannot be reversed.

questions.q: Salt dissolves in water to make salt solution. Which substance is the solvent?
questions.e: The solvent is the liquid that the solid dissolves in: water. Salt is the solute.

questions.q: Huda dissolves 20 g of sugar in 150 g of water. All of the sugar dissolves. What is the mass of the solution?
questions.e: Mass of solution = 150 g + 20 g = 170 g. The sugar is still there, so its mass is not lost.

questions.q: Ali has a mixture of sand and water. Which is the best way to get the sand back?
questions.e: Sand is insoluble, so filter paper traps the sand and lets the water through. A magnet only attracts magnetic materials such as iron; freezing would make a block of sandy ice.

questions.q: Describe how you can get salt crystals back from salt solution. Explain why this works.
questions.ms: 1 mark: heat the solution (in an evaporating basin) / leave it in a warm place so the water evaporates. 1 mark: the water turns into water vapour (gas) but the salt does not, so the salt is left behind as crystals. Do not accept: filter the solution.
questions.e: Heat the solution gently (or leave it somewhere warm and sunny). The water evaporates and leaves as water vapour, but the salt cannot evaporate at this temperature, so salt crystals are left in the basin. This shows dissolving is reversible.

questions.p:
Question 6
Sara investigates how the temperature of water affects the time a sugar cube takes to dissolve.
Her results: 20 °C → 150 s; 30 °C → 120 s; 40 °C → 120 s; 50 °C → 70 s; 60 °C → 45 s.
questions.q: (a) What is the independent variable (the variable Sara changes)?
questions.e: Sara chooses and changes the temperature of the water, so temperature is the independent variable.

questions.p:
Question 6
Sara investigates how the temperature of water affects the time a sugar cube takes to dissolve.
Her results: 20 °C → 150 s; 30 °C → 120 s; 40 °C → 120 s; 50 °C → 70 s; 60 °C → 45 s.
questions.q: (b) What is the dependent variable (the variable Sara measures)?
ans: how long it takes to dissolve
time for the sugar to dissolve
time taken for the sugar to dissolve
questions.e: She measures the time the sugar cube takes to dissolve, so time is the dependent variable.

questions.p:
Question 6
Sara investigates how the temperature of water affects the time a sugar cube takes to dissolve.
Her results: 20 °C → 150 s; 30 °C → 120 s; 40 °C → 120 s; 50 °C → 70 s; 60 °C → 45 s.
questions.q: (c) Write down two variables Sara must keep the same to make it a fair test.
questions.ms: 1 mark each, any two: volume of water; size/mass of sugar cube; type of sugar; amount/speed of stirring (or no stirring); same type/size of container. Do not accept: temperature; time.
questions.e: Any two of: the volume of water, the size (mass) of the sugar cube, the type of sugar, how much she stirs, the container. Temperature cannot be a control — it is the variable she changes.

questions.p:
Question 6
Sara investigates how the temperature of water affects the time a sugar cube takes to dissolve.
Her results: 20 °C → 150 s; 30 °C → 120 s; 40 °C → 120 s; 50 °C → 70 s; 60 °C → 45 s.
questions.q: (d) One result is anomalous (does not fit the pattern). At which temperature was it measured? Give the number in °C.
questions.e: The times should fall each time the temperature rises. At 40 °C the time (120 s) is the same as at 30 °C instead of being shorter (about 95 s would fit), so the 40 °C result is anomalous. Sara should repeat it.

questions.p:
Question 6
Sara investigates how the temperature of water affects the time a sugar cube takes to dissolve.
Her results: 20 °C → 150 s; 30 °C → 120 s; 40 °C → 120 s; 50 °C → 70 s; 60 °C → 45 s.
questions.q: (e) Which is the best conclusion from Sara's results?
c: The colder the water, the faster the sugar dissolves.
Temperature has no effect on dissolving.
Sugar melts faster in hot water.
The higher the temperature, the shorter the time to dissolve.
questions.e: Apart from the anomalous result, the time goes down as the temperature goes up. C uses the wrong word: sugar dissolves, it does not melt.

questions.q: Use the particle model to explain why sugar dissolves faster in hot water than in cold water.
questions.ms: 1 mark: (water) particles move faster / have more energy in hot water. 1 mark: they hit/collide with the sugar more often or harder, so sugar particles are pulled away / spread out more quickly. Do not accept: the sugar melts.
questions.e: In hot water the water particles have more energy and move faster. They bump into the sugar more often and with more force, so sugar particles are pulled off the crystal and spread out between the water particles more quickly.

questions.q: Ahmed says: "The sugar has melted in my tea." Which answer is correct?
c: Ahmed is right — hot tea melts sugar.
Ahmed is wrong — the sugar has dissolved; melting is one substance turning from solid to liquid.
Ahmed is wrong — the sugar has evaporated.
Ahmed is wrong — the sugar has reacted to make a new substance.
questions.e: Sugar in tea dissolves: its particles spread out between the water particles. Melting needs heat to turn one substance from solid to liquid (sugar melts only at a much higher temperature). No new substance is made, so it is not a reaction.

questions.p:
Question 12
A class added sugar, one spoonful at a time, to 100 ml of water at different temperatures until no more would dissolve.

questions.q: How many more spoonfuls dissolved at 80 °C than at 20 °C?
questions.e: From the bar chart: 80 °C → 9 spoonfuls; 20 °C → 4 spoonfuls. 9 − 4 = 5 more spoonfuls. This shows more solid dissolves at higher temperatures.

questions.q: Which pair are both reversible changes?
questions.e: Freezing (warm it to melt it) and dissolving (evaporate the water) can both be reversed. Each other pair contains a chemical change — burning, cooking or baking — that makes new substances.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Reversible physical change = no new substance, and you can get the original back (melting/freezing, evaporating/condensing, dissolving).
Solute + solvent → solution. Mass of solution = mass of solute + mass of solvent.
Filter to remove an insoluble solid; evaporate to get back a dissolved solid.
Hotter liquid → solid dissolves faster and more of it can dissolve.
Particle reason: hotter particles move faster, hit the solid more often and harder, and pull its particles away more quickly.
Sugar dissolves — it does not melt.
